Formal language

Words: 245 Articles: 6
Theoretical computer science OurBigBook.com
A formal language is a set of finite strings over a fixed finite alphabet.

L-system

Words: 51
Formal language OurBigBook.com
A parallel string-rewriting system: at each generation, every symbol is replaced simultaneously by its assigned word. Symbols can also encode drawing commands such as moving forward or turning. Large recursively defined drawings can be queried without expanding the whole word by precomputing the length, displacement, and rotation of each expanded block.

Binary string ({0,1}<ω)

Words: 133 Articles: 2
Formal language OurBigBook.com
A binary string is a finite word over the alphabet {0,1}. There are 2n strings of length n. Finite binary strings have an effective bijection with natural numbers, so computable enumerability and immunity apply to sets of strings.

Counting binary strings with bounded ones (#{w:#0(w)=n, #1(w)≤m}=(mn+m+1​))

Words: 51
Binary string OurBigBook.com
A binary string with n zeroes and j ones is determined by its j one-positions, giving (jn+j​) possibilities. Sum for 0≤j≤m and apply the hockey-stick identity. Equivalently, distribute at most m ones among the n+1 gaps around the zeroes and add a slack count; stars and bars counts n+2 nonnegative counts summing to m.

Self-delimiting binary code

Words: 48
Binary string OurBigBook.com
A self-delimiting code permits a decoder to identify the end of a code without an external length marker. Encoding a binary word of length ℓ by ℓ ones, a zero and the word uses 2ℓ+1 bits. This yields an O(logn) description of a natural number in an incompressibility proof.

Concatenation of formal languages (LM={uv:u∈L, v∈M})

Words: 27
Formal language OurBigBook.com
For formal languages L,M over the same alphabet, concatenate each word over an alphabet in L with each word over an alphabet in M. This operation is associative, has identity {ε} and absorbing element the empty language.

Empty language (∅)

Words: 20
Formal language OurBigBook.com
The formal language containing no words over an alphabet. It differs from the language containing only the empty word, which is a multiplicative identity for concatenation of formal languages.

Turing machine

Words: 835 Articles: 19
Theoretical computer science OurBigBook.com
A Turing machine is an abstract computational model with a finite control, an unbounded tape and a head that reads, writes and moves on the tape.

Blank symbol (□)

Words: 30
Turing machine OurBigBook.com
A designated tape alphabet symbol occupying unused cells of a Turing machine. It is excluded from the input alphabet, so a finite input word occupies a finite region of an otherwise blank tape.

Turing machine encoding (enc(M))

Words: 47
Turing machine OurBigBook.com
A finite string describing a Turing machine's states, alphabets, transition rules and designated initial and halting states. Standard encodings have a decidable language of valid descriptions. A syntactic property of an encoding need not be an extensional property of programs; for example, adding an unreachable state changes state count without changing the accepted formal language.

Multitape Turing machine

Words: 39
Turing machine OurBigBook.com
A Turing machine with a fixed finite number of tapes and a head for each tape. One transition reads the scanned symbols, updates them and moves the heads. This model accepts the same computably enumerable languages as a single-tape Turing machine, but step counts can differ.

Single-tape Turing machine

Words: 34
Turing machine OurBigBook.com
A Turing machine with one read-write tape. Every multitape Turing machine can be simulated by a single-tape Turing machine, using delimited tape portions and marked head positions. The simulation preserves the accepted formal language and whether a computation halts, while possibly increasing time complexity.

Read-only-from-left Turing acceptor

Words: 49
Turing machine OurBigBook.com
A deterministic single-tape Turing machine that leaves every scanned symbol unchanged and moves one cell right after every nonhalting transition. Such machines decide exactly the regular languages. A deterministic finite automaton simulates the finite control, with accepting states determined by the blank-only continuation after the input; conversely, a machine simulating a deterministic finite automaton halts on the first blank.

Instantaneous description of a Turing machine (C)

Words: 90 Articles: 1
Turing machine OurBigBook.com
An instantaneous description records the current control state, head position, and tape contents. For a tape blank outside a finite window, a word huqvh records the symbols u to the left of the head and v from the scanned cell rightward, with unrecorded cells blank. If v is empty, the head scans an implicit blank. Extra outer blanks can represent the same infinite tape. The instruction of a Turing machine determines its successor description.

Next-configuration relation (C⊢M​C′)

Words: 21
Instantaneous description of a Turing machine OurBigBook.com
For a Turing machine, the one-step binary relation between Turing machine configurations specified by its Turing machine instructions. Its reflexive transitive closure ⊢M∗​ describes any finite number of computation steps, including zero.

Instruction of a Turing machine (δ(q,a)=(p,b,D))

Words: 72
Turing machine OurBigBook.com
For a deterministic single-tape Turing machine, an instruction reads a state q and scanned tape symbol a, writes b, changes state to p, and moves the head one cell left, one cell right, or not at all according to D. The state and tape alphabets are finite; an undefined transition halts. A dedicated terminal state can be introduced by directing undefined transitions to it without changing whether computation halts.

Two-stack encoding of a Turing tape (c=(q,L,R))

Words: 56
Turing machine OurBigBook.com
Encode the cells immediately left of the head in a reversed positional stack L, and the current and right cells in R. Quotient and remainder by the alphabet base read and remove cells; multiplication by that base pushes a cell. The resulting local tape transitions are primitive recursive, which makes them directly implementable on Church numerals.

Modular machine (M)

Words: 183 Articles: 2
Turing machine OurBigBook.com
A modular machine of modulus m>1 acts on pairs in N2. Each instruction (a,b,c,R) or (a,b,c,L) has 0≤a,b<m and 0≤c<m2, and at most one instruction is assigned to each residue pair (a,b). The two transition types are (mu+a,mv+b)↦(m2u+c,v) and (mu+a,mv+b)↦(u,m2v+c). These finite arithmetic operations can encode a Turing machine; a designated terminal configuration can have a nonrecursive halting set.

Group encoding of a modular machine

Words: 73
Modular machine OurBigBook.com
A modular machine can be encoded by HNN extensions of K=Z2∗⟨t⟩. The kernel of K→Z2 has a free basis of a group t(r,s)=x−ry−stxrys. Associated-subgroup maps send these basis elements according to the two arithmetic transition types. In the resulting group, membership of t(r,s) in the subgroup generated by t and the instruction stable letters is equivalent to (r,s)∈H0​(M). One more HNN extension centralizes that finitely generated subgroup, converting membership to equality and hence to the word problem for a group.

Halting set at a designated terminal configuration (H0​(M))

Words: 46
Modular machine OurBigBook.com
For a modular machine whose (0,0) is terminal, H0​(M) is the set of configurations whose forward computation reaches exactly (0,0), including the zero-step computation there. It may differ from the set of configurations stopping at any terminal configuration. Determinism makes membership invariant along each instruction edge.

Deterministic computation

Words: 15
Turing machine OurBigBook.com
In a deterministic computation, every configuration and input symbol determine at most one next configuration.

Reversible computation

Words: 56 Articles: 1
Turing machine OurBigBook.com
A reversible computation has an injective transition function, so its preceding configuration can be recovered from its current configuration. Any finite classical computation can be simulated reversibly while retaining enough workspace to uncompute its temporary results.

Reversible circuit

Words: 20
Reversible computation OurBigBook.com
A reversible circuit is composed of bijective gates. The Toffoli gate is universal for reversible Boolean computation when ancillary bits are available.

Nondeterministic Turing machine

Words: 18
Turing machine OurBigBook.com
A nondeterministic computation may have several possible next configurations and accepts when at least one computation path accepts.

Oracle machine

Words: 120 Articles: 2
Turing machine OurBigBook.com
An oracle machine may query membership in a fixed language in one computation step.

Function oracle

Words: 87
Oracle machine OurBigBook.com
A function oracle supplies access to an unknown function f: given an allowed input x, one query returns f(x). Query complexity counts these accesses separately from known local computation. A classical query receives one definite answer; a quantum oracle specifies coherent access through a unitary operator, allowing inputs in quantum superposition. The distinction is part of the access model, not a change to the mathematical function.
A Boolean quantum oracle preserves x and adds a one-bit value f(x) into an answer qubit by exclusive or. On known computational-basis states, its output determines the same value as a classical function oracle query.

Relativization (complexity theory)

Words: 19
Oracle machine OurBigBook.com
A relativized complexity class CA allows every machine defining C to query the same oracle A.

Boolean operation (f:{0,1}n→{0,1})

Words: 1k Articles: 7
Theoretical computer science OurBigBook.com
A Boolean operation is a Boolean function taking truth values encoded as bits: 0 means false and 1 means true. These operations supply the concrete two-valued interpretation of a Boolean algebra. A Boolean valuation fixes the inputs; a truth table lists every possible input. With two input bits there are four rows.
The basic logical connectives are logical conjunction (AND, P∧Q, both true), logical disjunction (OR, P∨Q, at least one true), exclusive or (XOR, P⊕Q, exactly one true), and logical negation (NOT, ¬P, the opposite value). OR is inclusive: it accepts the case where both inputs are true.[ref]
For an original program-condition example, let P mean “the backup is recent” and Q mean “the backup is verified”. A rule requiring a recent, verified backup uses logical conjunction; one accepting either qualification uses logical disjunction. A rule flagging a mismatch between the two qualifications uses exclusive or. A recent, verified backup gives (P,Q)=(1,1): AND and OR accept it, while XOR does not flag it. The last row of the truth table makes this difference explicit.
The same small Boolean operations build larger tests and Boolean circuits. In a programming language, the value of a condition and the procedure for evaluating it both matter. For Boolean operands, Python's and, or, and not implement these logical connectives. Evaluation proceeds from the left; and skips its right operand if the left is false, and or skips it if the left is true. More generally, and and or return an operand, whereas not returns a Boolean.[ref]
For example, the Python condition denominator != 0 and numerator / denominator > 2 avoids division by zero because the logical conjunction's second test is evaluated only when the first succeeds. Reversing the tests preserves the abstract truth table for defined operands but can raise a division-by-zero error handled through exception handling. A rewrite involving a side effect must also preserve the needed evaluation behavior.

Boolean operations on events

Words: 110
Boolean operation OurBigBook.com
Events turn Boolean operations into operations on sets. For a die with sample space U={1,2,3,4,5,6}, let A={2,4,6} be the event “even outcome” and B={4,5,6} the event “outcome at least four”. At outcome u, use the indicator functions P=1A​(u) and Q=1B​(u). Then
AND: A∩BXOR: A△B​={4,6},={2,5},​OR: A∪BNOT A: U∖A​={2,4,5,6},={1,3,5}.​
(1)
Thus logical conjunction becomes set intersection, logical disjunction becomes set union, exclusive or becomes symmetric difference, and logical negation becomes the complement of a set within U. Outcome four satisfies both events, so inclusive logical disjunction includes it and exclusive or excludes it. If the die is fair, these four events have probabilities 1/3, 2/3, 1/3, and 1/2, respectively. No assumption of independent events is needed for the set identities; indeed A and B here are not independent, since 1/3=(1/2)(1/2).

Exclusive or (XOR, P⊕Q)

Words: 291 Articles: 1
Boolean operation OurBigBook.com
Exclusive or returns one exactly when its two input bits differ. Its truth table gives 0⊕0=0, 0⊕1=1, 1⊕0=1, and 1⊕1=0. The identities
P⊕Q=(P∨Q)∧¬(P∧Q)=(P∧¬Q)∨(¬P∧Q)
(2)
express exclusive or using logical conjunction, logical disjunction, and logical negation. The first expression accepts at least one input and then excludes both; the second explicitly lists the two accepted input pairs.
For numerical bits, exclusive or is addition in modular arithmetic modulo two:
x⊕y=(x+y)mod2.
(3)
The binary operation is commutative and associative, because addition modulo two has those properties. It satisfies x⊕0=x, x⊕1=¬x, and x⊕x=0. These identities explain why a bit can be toggled and restored with the same operation.
On binary strings of equal length, bitwise exclusive or applies the one-bit rule separately at each position. For example,
1010⊕0110=1100,1100⊕0110=1010.
(4)
A bit mask of 0110 toggles exactly the middle two bits. Applying the mask twice restores the original binary string: each selected bit changes twice, and each unselected bit stays fixed. This positional operation is distinct from taking the exclusive or of the overall truth values of two integers.

Exclusive or toggles and parity

Words: 135
Exclusive or OurBigBook.com
For bits x1​,…,xn​, repeated exclusive or computes the parity of the number of ones:
x1​⊕⋯⊕xn​=(∑i=1n​xi​)mod2.
(5)
An induction proves this: the first bit gives its own parity, and appending a zero preserves it while appending a one changes it. The binary string 10110 has three ones, so its parity bit is one. Append that parity bit to obtain 101101, whose six bits have even parity. Flipping the second bit produces 111101 and changes the combined exclusive or to one, detecting an error. Flipping the third bit as well produces 110101, with four ones and combined exclusive or zero: an even number of flips can escape this check.
For three inputs, repeated exclusive or means an odd number of true inputs, rather than exactly one: 1⊕1⊕1=1. The “exactly one” description applies to the two-input exclusive or. This distinction matters when translating a requirement that exactly one option be selected into a program condition.

Negation (¬P)

Words: 108 Articles: 1
Boolean operation OurBigBook.com
Logical negation exchanges zero and one: ¬0=1 and ¬1=0. For a numerical bit x, this is 1−x; applying logical negation twice restores x. It acts on the entire propositional formula in its scope. Parentheses therefore matter: ¬(P∨Q) says that neither condition holds, while (¬P)∨Q also accepts every case where Q holds. At (P,Q)=(1,1) their values are zero and one.
On a set, logical negation becomes taking a complement in a fixed universal set. In Boolean operations on events, “not even” selects {1,3,5}. “Not both even and at least four” selects {1,2,3,5}; it does not require both qualifications to fail. De Morgan's laws make the scope of these compound negations precise.

De Morgan's laws (¬(P∧Q)≡¬P∨¬Q)

Words: 443 Articles: 1
Boolean operation OurBigBook.com
De Morgan's laws exchange logical conjunction and logical disjunction when a logical negation moves across them:
¬(P∧Q)≡(¬P)∨(¬Q),¬(P∨Q)≡(¬P)∧(¬Q).
(6)
Here ≡ denotes logical equivalence: the two propositional formulas agree under every Boolean valuation.[ref]
A complete verification uses the four rows of a truth table. In input order (0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1), both sides of the first logical equivalence have output sequence (1,1,1,0); both sides of the second have (1,0,0,0). A proof in words is equally short: failure of “both” means at least one failure, whereas failure of “at least one” means both fail. The differing middle rows explain why simply pushing logical negation inward without changing AND to OR is wrong.
For the events in Boolean operations on events, the corresponding set identities are
U∖(A∩B)=(U∖A)∪(U∖B)={1,2,3,5},
(7)
U∖(A∪B)=(U∖A)∩(U∖B)={1,3}.
(8)
One can prove these identities by checking an arbitrary set element u∈U: its two membership truth values obey De Morgan's laws. The same reasoning works for any two subsets of a common universal set.
For a nested program test, let R mean “backup recent”, V mean “backup verified”, and O mean “manual override authorized”. Rejecting when neither an acceptable backup nor an override is present gives
¬((R∧V)∨O)≡((¬R)∨(¬V))∧¬O.
(9)
The transformed condition reads “backup stale or unverified, and no override”. Apply the second of De Morgan's laws at the outside, then the first at the inner logical conjunction. For (R,V,O)=(1,0,0) it rejects; changing only O to one makes it accept. With Boolean operands in Python, not ((recent and verified) or override) and ((not recent) or (not verified)) and (not override) have the same result and inspect the operands in the same order, with the same skipped operands.

De Morgan dual of a Boolean function (f∗(x)=¬f(¬x))

Words: 141
De Morgan's laws OurBigBook.com
For a Boolean function f of n input bits, define its De Morgan dual by complementing every input, applying f, and complementing the output:
f∗(x1​,…,xn​)=1−f(1−x1​,…,1−xn​).
(10)
De Morgan's laws say that the De Morgan dual of logical conjunction is logical disjunction, and conversely. The constant zero Boolean function becomes constant one. This is different from merely negating the output: for AND, output logical negation gives one at (0,0), whereas the De Morgan dual gives zero there.
Taking the De Morgan dual twice restores the original Boolean function:
(f∗)∗(x)=1−(1−f(x))=f(x).
(11)
Here each input is complemented twice as well. For a Boolean formula built from AND, OR, NOT and constants, its De Morgan dual can therefore be obtained by exchanging AND with OR and zero with one throughout, leaving input names and NOT in place. A structural induction proves the rule: it holds for an input and each constant, De Morgan's laws handle the two binary logical connectives, and double logical negation handles NOT. This symmetry lets one translate a complex test systematically instead of guessing where its failures occur.

Theoretical computer science OurBigBook.com
Computational complexity theory classifies computational problems by the resources needed to solve them.

Bit complexity

Words: 50
Computational complexity theory OurBigBook.com
The number of elementary operations on bits required by an algorithm. Arithmetic-operation counts treat operations on entire integers as units, whereas bit complexity charges for the sizes of their operands. An algorithm using few multiplications can therefore require substantially more bit operations when the operands grow. State the model when comparing bounds for repeated squaring or dynamic programming counts.

Parameterized complexity

Words: 192 Articles: 2
Computational complexity theory OurBigBook.com
Parameterized complexity studies an algorithm's resource use as a function of both the encoded input length N and a distinguished nonnegative integer parameter k. A small solution size, a dimension or a structural property of a graph can serve as the parameter. Fixed-parameter tractability allows arbitrary computable dependence on k while keeping the exponent of N independent of k.

Kernelization

Words: 81
Parameterized complexity OurBigBook.com
A kernelization is a polynomial-time algorithm mapping a parameterized decision problem instance (I,k) to an equivalent instance (I′,k′) of the same problem, with both encoded length ∣I′∣ and parameter k′ bounded by a computable function of k. Equivalent means that both instances have the same yes/no answer. The bound need not be a polynomial in k; a polynomial kernel is the stronger requirement that it is. For a decidable problem, exhaustively solving the bounded output leaves only a computable dependence on k, so kernelization yields fixed-parameter tractability.

Fixed-parameter tractability (f(k)NO(1))

Words: 58
Parameterized complexity OurBigBook.com
A parameterized decision problem is fixed-parameter tractable if an algorithm decides every instance of encoded length N and parameter k in running time at most f(k)Nc, for a computable function f and a constant c independent of k. The distinction is in the exponent: 2kN3 has this form, whereas an Nk bound alone does not establish fixed-parameter tractability. Branching on an uncovered edge gives a fixed-parameter tractable vertex cover decision problem.

Element distinctness problem

Words: 66
Computational complexity theory OurBigBook.com
Decide whether all input elements are distinct. In the comparison model, this needs Ω(nlogn) comparisons in the worst case. An accepting decision-tree leaf for distinct keys must force a total order: incomparable keys could otherwise be made equal consistently with its strict comparison outcomes. Thus the n! possible orders require different accepting leaves, giving a decision-tree depth of at least log3​(n!)=Ω(nlogn) even for three-way comparisons.

Comparison model

Words: 103 Articles: 1
Computational complexity theory OurBigBook.com
A model in which an algorithm learns the relative order or equality of input keys by comparisons. Lower-bound reductions must preserve the information available to each comparison; transforming numbers and allowing stronger tests without justification can change the model. For intervals (2zi​,2zi​+1) built from integers, every endpoint comparison can be simulated by comparing original keys and then fixed offsets.

Ternary comparison

Comparison model OurBigBook.com
A single comparison returning one of three outcomes: less than, equal to, or greater than. A comparison model may count this as one operation even when a programming language expresses the outcomes using multiple Boolean tests. Binary search on ordered keys uses one such comparison per inspected position.

Equivalence of weighted formula utility representations

Words: 68
Computational complexity theory OurBigBook.com
Given two weighted formula utility representations with binary rational numbers as weights, decide whether their values agree on every Boolean valuation. This problem is co-NP-complete.
For membership, a valuation witnessing unequal values certifies non-equivalence. Evaluate all propositional formulas and add their weights exactly in polynomial time. For hardness, compare the one-rule base {(θ,1)} with the empty base. They are equivalent exactly when θ is an unsatisfiable Boolean formula. Thus even very small weighted rule bases express a universal equivalence question.

co-NP (coNP={L:L∈NP})

Words: 47
Computational complexity theory OurBigBook.com
The class of decision problems whose complements belong to NP. Equivalently, negative instances admit polynomially bounded witnesses verifiable in polynomial time. A problem is co-NP-complete when it is in co-NP and every problem in co-NP has a polynomial-time reduction to it. Unsatisfiability of a propositional formula is a basic example: its complement is the NP-complete Boolean satisfiability problem.

Query complexity (Q(f))

Words: 331 Articles: 2
Computational complexity theory OurBigBook.com
The number of accesses to an unknown input needed to solve a specified task. The input might be a string with individually readable entries, or an implicitly supplied function. A complete statement specifies deterministic, randomized, or quantum access, the accepted error, and worst-case or expected cost. Quantum query complexity permits coherent input access through a quantum oracle.

Identification of a unique essential variable (d+⌈log2​n⌉ queries suffice)

Words: 134
Query complexity OurBigBook.com
Suppose an unknown function on {1,…,d}n has exactly one essential variable. Query the diagonal inputs (t,…,t) to find two coordinates values a,b giving distinct outputs; at most d function-evaluation oracle calls suffice because the unary dependence is nonconstant. A query taking value b on an index subset H and a outside it then tests whether the essential coordinate lies in H. Repeated halving locates it in at most ⌈log2​n⌉ further queries. If n=1, no query is needed.
For a matching lower bound with fixed d, restrict to f(i)(x)=1 when xi​=1 and 2 otherwise. Every query has only two possible replies. A binary decision tree distinguishing the n possible essential indices needs at least n leaves and depth ⌈log2​n⌉. Integer outputs in the unrestricted problem need not be binary; the restricted family is what makes this query complexity argument valid.

Classical query complexity of linear Boolean function identification (D(n)=n)

Words: 144
Query complexity OurBigBook.com
In exact classical identification of an unknown linear Boolean function fa​(x)=a⋅x, a function oracle call returns one bit fa​(x). The query complexity is exactly n for n≥1. Queries on the standard basis inputs ej​ reveal aj​, proving sufficiency. For necessity, a depth-k decision tree has at most 2k answer histories and must distinguish 2n hidden binary strings; hence k≥n, even with adaptive inputs. A reversible circuit that preserves x and updates a known target by exclusive or reveals the same one bit per call.
There is also a useful linear algebra proof. Along a fixed history, the chosen inputs form the rows of a matrix M over the two-element finite field, and the replies specify Ma. If there are k<n queries, the rank-nullity theorem gives a nonzero vector v with Mv=0. Then a and a+v give identical replies throughout this history. This also explains why adaptive choices cannot evade the bound: equal earlier replies force the same later choices.

Communication complexity

Words: 153 Articles: 1
Computational complexity theory OurBigBook.com
Communication complexity studies how much information distributed parties must exchange to compute a function of their separately held inputs. Local computation is free; the resource being counted is communicated bits or qubits, with the allowed shared randomness, quantum entanglement or other correlations specified separately. For a Boolean function f(x,y), a one-way exact protocol has the receiver output f correctly for every input after a single message. One-bit computation using Popescu–Rohrlich boxes shows that this resource measure changes drastically if ideal superquantum boxes are available.

Communication complexity OurBigBook.com
For even positive n, share the maximally entangled state ∣Ω⟩=n−1/2∑i=0n−1​∣ii⟩. Each party applies a phase oracle from its input binary string, producing ∣Ωxy​⟩=n−1/2∑i​(−1)xi​+yi​∣ii⟩. Its overlap with ∣Ω⟩ is the displayed expression because the Hamming distance counts exactly the negative signs. Under the promise dH​(x,y)∈{0,n/2}, the output either equals ∣Ω⟩ or is orthogonal to it. Sending one subsystem lets the receiver distinguish the cases with the projective measurement {∣Ω⟩⟨Ω∣,I−∣Ω⟩⟨Ω∣}. The transmitted system needs ⌈log2​n⌉ qubits, including when n is not a power of two.

Computational complexity theory OurBigBook.com
A promise problem consists of disjoint sets of YES and NO instances. An algorithm or verifier must obey its correctness guarantees only on their union. Energy problems with separated thresholds are naturally promise problems because intermediate-energy instances require no prescribed answer.

Quantum complexity theory studies resources needed by quantum circuits and quantum algorithms, including time, workspace, and quantum query complexity. Its models specify which input oracles and gate implementations are available; counting oracle calls is different from counting all elementary gates.

BQP (BQP)

Quantum complexity theory OurBigBook.com
BQP is the class of promise problems decided by uniform polynomial-size quantum circuits with bounded error. Completeness 2/3 and soundness 1/3 are conventional; BQP error reduction shows that other fixed separated thresholds give the same class.
BQP error reduction
Words: 51
BQP OurBigBook.com
Independent runs of a BQP algorithm with fresh ancilla qubits can be combined by a classical threshold rule. If completeness exceeds soundness by γ, a Hoeffding inequality bounds the error after r runs by e−rγ2/2. Polynomial repetition handles inverse-polynomial gaps. This does not automatically preserve the restricted gate and measurement rules of a stoquastic circuit.

Quantum complexity theory OurBigBook.com
A quantum witness is a polynomial-size quantum state supplied to a verifier as evidence for a YES instance. The verifier fixes its own ancilla qubits independently. Pure quantum witnesses suffice when maximizing a linear acceptance functional on density operators. Quantum witnesses are not generally restricted to basis vectors or product states.

StoqMA (StoqMA(a,b),1/2≤b<a≤1)

Words: 71
Quantum complexity theory OurBigBook.com
StoqMA is a restricted quantum-verifier class using stoquastic circuits and polynomial-size quantum witnesses. A YES instance has a quantum witness accepted with probability at least a; on a NO instance every quantum witness has acceptance at most b, with an inverse-polynomial gap a−b. An optimal quantum witness can be chosen with nonnegative amplitudes, since the witness acceptance operator is entrywise nonnegative. The quantum witness is generally a superposition, rather than a computational basis vector. The stoquastic acceptance floor explains the lower limit b≥1/2 for a nontrivial soundness promise.

QMA

Words: 350 Articles: 5
Quantum complexity theory OurBigBook.com
QMA is the class of promise problems with a polynomial-size quantum witness checked by a uniform polynomial-size quantum circuit. YES instances have an accepting witness with probability at least 2/3; NO instances have acceptance at most 1/3 for every witness, including mixed states. The verifier's acceptance is linear in the witness density operator. Inverse-polynomial or exponentially small error can be obtained through QMA error reduction.

Known gates and workspace operations are not counted as oracle queries, although they contribute to the circuit's full runtime. An efficient query bound therefore need not, by itself, be an efficient gate bound.

Quantum query complexity OurBigBook.com
A quantum oracle supplies coherent access to a function through a specified unitary operator. For a function with binary string output, the standard construction retains the input and adds the output into an answer quantum register by bitwise exclusive or. This operation is its own inverse, even when the function is not injective. A Boolean quantum oracle is the single-output-bit case; Simon's algorithm uses several answer qubits. Other encodings, such as a modular-addition quantum oracle or a phase gate encoding, require their own explicit query conventions.
Phase oracle (Of​∣x⟩=(−1)f(x)∣x⟩)
Words: 148 Articles: 1
Quantum oracle OurBigBook.com
A phase oracle encodes a Boolean function in the signs of computational basis states. Its diagonal entries have modulus one, so it is a unitary operator. The usual convention Of​ changes the sign when f(x)=1. A complemented convention Uf​∣x⟩=(−1)f(x)⊕1∣x⟩ instead changes the sign when f(x)=0, with Uf​=−Of​; ⊕ denotes exclusive or. The two conventions differ by a global phase when used without coherent control, but the global phase of a controlled quantum gate makes that difference observable when the quantum oracle is controlled.

An unrestricted Boolean function on M>2 inputs cannot be classified as constant or nonconstant with certainty using a single phase oracle query, even with quantum ancillas. Write a purified query input as ∣Ψ⟩=∑x​∣x⟩∣ax​⟩ with px​=∥ax​∥2 and ∑x​px​=1. The zero constant function leaves it unchanged; the function supported only at j produces a vector with inner product 1−2pj​ with it. Perfect discrimination of pure states requires orthogonality, forcing pj​=1/2 for all j and thus M=2, a contradiction. This is an exact quantum query complexity obstruction for all nonconstant inputs, rather than the restricted promise used by the Deutsch-Jozsa algorithm.

After T input-bit queries, every probability amplitude is a polynomial of degree at most T, because the bit-query matrix entries are affine in the input bits. An acceptance probability is a sum of squared absolute amplitudes and has polynomial degree at most 2T. Multilinear reduction on the Boolean cube does not increase degree. Exact acceptance therefore implies QE​(f)≥⌈deg(f)/2⌉. For bounded error the acceptance polynomial only approximates the Boolean function; its exact representing degree is not the relevant bound.

The least worst-case number of input-oracle calls made by a quantum circuit that computes a Boolean function with zero error on every input. Known unitary gates and classical processing do not count toward this quantity; their runtime is a separate cost.

One exact parity query determines whether the first two bits agree. If they agree, a second query reads one of them; otherwise it reads the third bit. Those values respectively determine the three-bit majority function. The matching lower bound follows from its degree-three multilinear polynomial.

A compute-phase-uncompute construction marks those partners using two function queries and reversible table comparison. Known-subset Grover search then uses O((N−m)/m​) such phase queries. Including table preparation and a final verification query gives
T(m)=m+O(mN−m​​)+1.

Choosing m≍N1/3 balances both terms and gives T(m)=O(N1/3). The Grover rotation angle rounding bound gives success tending to one. This is a query bound; it does not make reversible table lookup free in a gate or physical-memory cost model.

Decision tree

Words: 1k Articles: 12
Decision tree model OurBigBook.com
A decision tree represents a deterministic computation of a known Boolean function f:{0,1}n→{0,1} by inspecting input bits. Each internal vertex of its binary tree names a coordinate i to query, its two outgoing edges carry answers 0 and 1, and each leaf carries the output 0 or 1. Starting at the root of a tree, read the named bit, follow its answer edge, and repeat until a leaf is reached. Correctness requires the leaf's label to equal f(x) for every input x.[ref]
The next coordinate, or the decision to stop, can depend on earlier answers: this is adaptive querying. The same input always follows the same graph path; adaptivity does not require randomness. A correct leaf must have the same output for every completion of the observed bits. Thus a decision tree can stop as soon as the observations form a query certificate. Querying an already known coordinate adds no information, so we use decision trees without repeated coordinates on a graph path; an efficient tree also removes queries made after the output is already forced.
The motivation is exact computation with shortcuts. If inspecting an input entry is expensive, the question is how much of the input must actually be read. The decision-tree query cost counts these inspections, while local calculations on known values are free in this model; this cost need not equal an implementation's time complexity. Here the Boolean function is specified in advance and must be computed exactly on every input. Decision tree learning instead fits a predictor from data, with a different objective.

Three-bit majority decision tree (MAJ3​)

Decision tree OurBigBook.com
Three votes give a small but revealing majority function:
m(x1​,x2​,x3​)={1,0,​x1​+x2​+x3​≥2,x1​+x2​+x3​<2.​
(13)
Our decision tree queries x1​, then x2​. If these bits agree, return their common value: two equal votes already force the majority function. If they disagree, query x3​ and return its value. The first two queries have a fixed order, but whether a third query occurs is adaptive.
Each internal label in the diagram names the next bit to inspect. Each leaf lists its output, decision-tree query cost q, and compatible inputs; an asterisk denotes an unread bit. The two shallow leaves each cover two inputs, while each deeper leaf covers one. Reading every bit would also compute the majority function, but would miss these exact shortcuts.
All eight inputs give the following exhaustive check. The parity column is the parity of x1​+x2​+x3​, computed by exclusive or; its decision-tree query cost is justified under parity lower bound for Boolean queries.
x1​x2​x3​Majority function outputQueried coordinates for the majority functionMajority function query countParity outputParity query count00001,220300101,221301001,2,331301111,2,330310001,2,331310111,2,330311011,220311111,2213
The worst inputs for this decision tree are 010,011,100,101, exactly those with x1​=x2​. Its actual depth is three. Every exact decision tree for this majority function has depth at least three: after the first query, an adversary can answer the second distinct query with the opposite bit, leaving the last bit decisive. Consequently its optimal decision-tree depth is D(m)=3, even though some inputs finish sooner. Every input has a two-bit query certificate, namely two agreeing votes; locating those votes can require a third query. This separates having a short query certificate from finding one.
Parity lower bound for Boolean queries (D(PARITYn​)=n)
Words: 117
Decision tree OurBigBook.com
For three bits, the Boolean function p(x)=x1​⊕x2​⊕x3​ outputs one when x1​+x2​+x3​ is odd, where ⊕ denotes exclusive or. Unlike the three-bit majority decision tree, an exact decision tree computing parity must inspect all three bits on every input. If any coordinate is unread, two completions differing only at that coordinate follow the same observed graph path but have opposite parity. A single leaf cannot correctly label both.
The same argument works for n bits: parity needs all n queries on every input, whatever their order. Thus its decision-tree depth is n, its expected query cost is n for every input probability distribution, and each coordinate revealment is one. The algorithm remains required to be correct on the whole Boolean cube, even if the chosen probability distribution assigns some inputs zero probability; a promise restricting permitted inputs would be a different computational problem.
Decision-tree query cost (qT​(x))
Words: 526 Articles: 2
Decision tree OurBigBook.com
For a particular decision tree T, its decision-tree query cost qT​(x) is the number of queries along the graph path followed by input x. Its actual tree depth is
h(T)=maxx∈{0,1}n​qT​(x).
(14)
The query vertices count as operations; each is followed by one answer edge. Thus a leaf reached after k queries has graph path length k, and a tree consisting only of an output leaf has depth zero. With no repeated coordinates, 0≤qT​(x)≤n. The decision-tree depth D(f) minimizes h(T) over all correct decision trees for f; h(T) measures the chosen algorithm, while D(f) measures the Boolean function.
Choose an input probability distribution μ and let X have that distribution. Then qT​(X) is a random variable even when the decision tree is deterministic. Its probability mass function describes how often each path length occurs, and its expected value is the expected query cost. None of these quantities changes the actual maximum depth of T.
The left panel aggregates the eight inputs from the three-bit majority decision tree: four cost two queries and four cost three. Parity always costs three. The right panel asks a different question, which coordinates are inspected: the majority function algorithm always queries coordinates 1 and 2, but queries coordinate 3 only on disagreements. These are probabilities of inspection, not probabilities that a bit equals one.
Expected query cost (Eμ​[qT​(X)])

Decision-tree query cost OurBigBook.com
For a fixed decision tree T and input probability distribution μ, its expected query cost is
Eμ​[qT​(X)]=∑x∈{0,1}n​μ(x)qT​(x).
(15)
Under the discrete uniform distribution on the eight three-bit inputs, the three-bit majority decision tree has
Pr(qT​(X)=2)=Pr(qT​(X)=3)=21​,E[qT​(X)]=2⋅21​+3⋅21​=25​=2.5.
(16)
This is an exact average, not a fractional query made during one execution. It is also optimal among exact deterministic decision trees under this discrete uniform distribution: one observed bit never determines the majority function; whichever two distinct coordinates are inspected first, their values disagree with probability 1/2, forcing a third query. In comparison, querying all three bits unconditionally has the same actual depth three but expected query cost three.
For an arbitrary input probability distribution, the same fixed three-bit majority decision tree gives Eμ​[qT​(X)]=2+Prμ​(X1​=X2​). A game tree evaluation rule using maxima at the controlled player’s decision nodes and expected values at chance nodes:
V(s)=maxa​V(T(s,a)),V(s)=∑s′​P(s′∣s)V(s′),
(20)
respectively. Terminal utilities fix the boundary values. These rules exactly optimize a finite-horizon expected utility objective by backward induction. For cyclic infinite-horizon reachability problems, a finite Markov decision process formulation and value iteration replace naive expansion of an infinite game tree. Start with one at successful terminal states and zero elsewhere, keep terminal values fixed, and apply the maximizing/expectation backups repeatedly. The tth iterate is the greatest success probability achievable within t transitions, by backward induction. These values are nondecreasing and bounded by one. For every policy, eventual success is the increasing set union of success within finite horizons, so its probability is the limit of those finite-horizon probabilities. Taking the supremum over policies and horizons in either order proves that the iterates converge to the optimal eventual-success probability. The limiting fixed-point equations can also admit larger solutions, so the initialization from terminal-success indicators matters.

Search problem OurBigBook.com
Two controlled walkers on the same connected undirected graph can each traverse one edge or wait in each unit-cost step. If they meet only by occupying the same vertex at the same time, their minimum meeting time is
⌈2d(p,q)​⌉,
(21)
where d is the shortest path distance. A common meeting point after t steps implies d(p,q)≤2t by the triangle inequality. Conversely, choose a middle vertex of a shortest connecting graph path; both walkers reach it within ⌈d/2⌉ steps, and the earlier arrival waits. The wait is essential when the path length is an odd integer. This distance on the joint Cartesian product state space is a consistent heuristic: each joint move changes the walkers’ separation by at most two. Replacing d by an obstacle-free Manhattan distance preserves admissible heuristic and consistent heuristic guarantees.

Sensorless planning chooses one action sequence that succeeds from every possible initial physical state without receiving distinguishing observations during execution. A belief state is a set of possibilities. For a deterministic search transition model T, an applicable action maps B to {T(s,a):s∈B}; for nondeterministic outcomes, take the union of all possible successors. Applicability must hold for every member of B, and success requires the resulting belief state to be a subset of the physical goal set.
Every fixed action sequence preserves inclusion of the initial belief states. Consequently, a successful plan for B also succeeds for every subset of B. Success on a superset is an additional requirement, so cannot be inferred from success on B alone. This property supports incremental belief-state search.

Sensorless planning OurBigBook.com
An incremental belief-state search initially plans for a small subset B0​ of the possible initial states, then tests the candidate plan on the full initial belief state B. If a state in B makes an action inapplicable or fails the final goal test, add that counterexample to B0​ and solve the enlarged problem. The new search may need to revise the entire plan, rather than append actions to the previous candidate.
With finitely many initial states and a complete finite-model solver for each restricted problem, at most ∣B∣ state additions are required. Failure to find a plan even for a restricted subset proves that none can work for the whole belief state. A candidate that passes full validation is a genuine plan for sensorless planning. The advantage is selective tracking: a small number of representative initial states may force a universally successful plan without constructing the full power set search space.

Every goal-reaching graph path then costs at least h1​+h2​ under its original costs. Taking the minimum proves admissibility without counting the same work twice.

For the maximum, choose an index attaining it at the source and bound its successor by the successor maximum. For the minimum, choose an index attaining it at the successor and bound the source minimum by that component. For a convex combination, multiply the two consistency inequalities by their nonnegative weights and add them. All these combinations vanish at goals when the inputs do.

Words: 189
Constraint satisfaction problem OurBigBook.com
A binary constraint satisfaction problem whose constraint graph is a tree. Restrict constraint domains by unary conditions first. Choose a rooted tree orientation and process children before parents. For each child j of i, retain in Di​ only values having a compatible value in the already reduced Dj​. Thus every retained parent value has support in each child subtree.
If the root constraint domain becomes empty, no solution exists. Otherwise choose any root value, then recursively choose supported child values. A child-to-parent arc consistency pass need not enforce full arc consistency in both directions; the chosen directional condition suffices for this construction.
The proof uses mathematical induction on subtrees. A retained leaf value satisfies its unary requirements. Each retained parent value has a supported value in every child subtree. Those subtree solutions can be combined because the tree has no edges between different child subtrees. Therefore every retained parent value extends to a whole subtree solution, and every retained root value extends to a complete solution without backtracking.
For N variables and maximum constraint domain size d, scanning all value pairs once per edge costs O(Nd2) time complexity in Big O notation, when one binary constraint evaluation has unit cost. If a constraint requires summing bundle values, its evaluation cost must also be counted.

Revising the arc i→j deletes unsupported values from Di​; it does not directly delete values from Dj​. Full arc consistency requires the condition in both directions on every edge of the constraint graph. On general graphs, it need not imply that a complete solution exists.

At O(d2) per revision plus O(v) per emptiness scan, a direct time complexity bound is O((vd+1)(ed2+v)). AC-3 uses a work list to avoid scanning unrelated arcs after each local change.

Mathematical induction shows that every revision preserves every such family E. At termination the current domains themselves satisfy arc consistency, so they are the greatest such family. If Di​ shrinks, incoming arcs k→i are reconsidered; the just-used neighbor j need not be included, since deleted values had no support in Dj​ and hence supported no surviving value there. Initially empty constraint domains are rejected before processing.
Each deletion preserves every complete solution: a solution using the removed value would supply its missing support. Therefore an empty constraint domain certifies impossibility. Successful termination establishes arc consistency but need not establish satisfiability. A triangle of two-valued inequality constraints supplies a counterexample: all values have pairwise support, but no assignment can satisfy all three inequalities.
For v variables, e constrained pairs and maximum constraint domain size d, assume constant-time compatibility tests for combined pair relations. A revision costs O(d2), and each shrinking source constraint domain can cause at most d rounds of reconsideration of its incoming arcs. Thus there are O(ed) revisions and time complexity O(v+ed3). Fixed d, including two-valued constraint domains, gives linear time in v+e.

Words: 2k Articles: 25
Complexity class OurBigBook.com
The time complexity of an algorithm bounds its number of computation steps as a function of its input length.
Specify both the size parameter and the operations counted. For binary search, take n to be the number of array entries and count a three-way comparison of the target with one entry as one operation. Code using separate equality and less-than tests may perform two primitive tests per inspected entry; this changes a constant factor. The input size in bits is a different parameter when entries have variable-length representations.
Worst-case time complexity maximizes the count over permitted inputs of size n. An absent target forces n comparisons in linear search. For binary search, the worst-case count is ⌊log2​n⌋+1 for n≥1, attained by a target larger than every entry. Both have a best case of one comparison when the first inspected entry matches.
In Big O notation, the worst-case bounds are O(n) and O(logn) respectively. Here T(n)=O(g(n)) means that fixed constants C,n0​ exist with T(n)≤Cg(n) for all n≥n0​. It is an upper bound, so a logarithmic count is also O(n); the sharper bound communicates its scaling better. The base of the logarithm changes only a constant factor.
For n=1,000,000, linear search can require 1,000,000 comparisons, whereas binary search needs at most 20, since 219≤n<220. Doubling n adds just one to the worst-case binary search count. These are operation counts, not measured machine runtimes. Translating them into logarithmic execution time assumes constant-cost indexed access, comparison and index arithmetic. Long entries can make comparison expensive; a linked list does not provide constant-cost access to an arbitrary middle index. Building or sorting the array is additional work: merge sort can provide order for many subsequent searches, but its cost belongs in the analysis too.

Amortized analysis (ci​=ci​+Φi​−Φi−1​)
Words: 1k Articles: 7
Time complexity OurBigBook.com
Amortized analysis bounds the total cost of every permitted sequence of operations from a specified initial state. An amortized O(1) bound means that some constants a,b satisfy ∑i=1m​ci​≤am+b for every such sequence of length m. The cost model and allowed operations are part of the claim; Big O notation alone does not specify them.
  • A worst-case bound for one operation limits its cost in any reachable state. Summing these separate maxima can overestimate the cost of a whole sequence because expensive states may take many cheap operations to rebuild.
  • An amortized analysis limits the total over every allowed sequence, including an unfavourably chosen one. Dividing that bound by the number of operations is a deterministic guarantee about the sequence.
  • A probabilistic average-case analysis bounds an expected value under a stated probability distribution on inputs. For a randomized algorithm, an expected value can instead average over its random choices. Neither interpretation is required by a deterministic amortized analysis.
This distinction, and the credit and potential method viewpoints, are developed in R. Endre Tarjan's 1985 paper Amortized Computational Complexity, sections 1–2, pp. 306–308. The dynamic array doubling example below shows how an expensive operation can pay for itself through the cheap operations that precede it.

The upper bound counts at most n cost at each active position; the lower bound uses ⌊x⌋≥x/2 for x≥1. This shows why exponential position costs cancel the decreasing carry frequencies that make the ordinary binary counter have constant amortized cost.

The bound a(n) is then an amortized per-operation time complexity. Dividing the total bound by m explains the averaging; it is a guarantee over every permitted sequence, without an assumed probability distribution on requests. Individual operations can cost more than a(n).
Dynamic array doubling (T(n)=n+Cn​−1)
Words: 479
Amortized analysis OurBigBook.com
Consider a dynamic array holding fixed-size entries. Its size n is the number of occupied slots and its capacity C is the number of allocated slots. Start with n=0, C=1. The only operation is append: if n=C, allocate a new array of capacity 2C, copy the C existing entries, and release the old array; then write the new entry and increase n by one. There is no reserve operation, deletion or shrinking in this model.
Count one unit for writing the new entry and one unit per existing entry copied during resizing. Thus the ith append has actual cost ci​=1 without resizing and ci​=C+1 when the old capacity C is full. Copying an entry, including its read and write, is one counted action. Allocation, deallocation, index arithmetic operations and the initial one-slot allocation are outside this exact count. If these add only a constant per ordinary append and a linear cost per resize, the Big O notation conclusions still hold, with different constants; costly entry copies require their own cost model.
The first ten costs are 1,2,3,1,5,1,1,1,9,1. For example, append 9 copies eight entries and writes one, so c9​=9. At that point the capacity becomes 16, but the total cost of all nine appends is only 24.
For n≥1, the final capacity is Cn​=2⌈log2​n⌉. Every earlier capacity 1,2,4,…,Cn​/2 was copied once. This geometric series sums to Cn​−1, including the empty sum when n=1. Therefore aggregate analysis gives the exact total
T(0)=0,T(n)=∑i=1n​ci​=n+Cn​−1,n≤Cn​<2n(n≥1).
(24)
Consequently T(n)<3n, so append has amortized O(1) cost in Big O notation for every prefix from this empty initial state. The values being appended do not affect the count. In contrast, an append to a full dynamic array with n entries costs n+1: its worst-case cost is O(n), and actually grows linearly along full-capacity states. A bound on total work does not promise a constant response time for each call.
The same policy controls computer memory: after each completed append, n≤Cn​<2n for n≥1, so fewer than n slots are unused. This is a bound on the retained backing array, with fixed-size slots. During a resize from full capacity k to 2k, a copying implementation can temporarily hold both arrays, totalling 3k allocated slots before releasing the old one. Thus the retained-capacity bound does not bound this temporary peak by twice the live size. Allocator metadata and separately allocated objects are additional computer memory costs.
The geometric series is the source of the efficiency. If capacity instead increases by one each time, the same count becomes n+1+2+⋯+(n−1)=n(n+1)/2, a quadratic total. Dynamic array doubling buys a linear total with bounded spare capacity, even when the final length is unknown.
Potential method (Φ(D))
Words: 371 Articles: 1
Amortized analysis OurBigBook.com
The potential method assigns a number Φ(D) to each state D of a data structure. Let Di​ be the state after operation i, Φi​=Φ(Di​), and ci​ its actual cost. Its amortized cost is the actual cost plus the change in potential. Summing and cancelling adjacent potentials gives a telescoping sum:
ci​=ci​+Φi​−Φi−1​,∑i=1m​ci​=∑i=1m​ci​+Φ0​−Φm​.
(25)
If Φ0​=0 and every reachable Φi​≥0, the sum of amortized costs bounds the actual total for every prefix. A nonzero initial potential contributes the explicit additive term Φ0​. Potential is proof bookkeeping; the algorithm need not store it.[ref]
For dynamic array doubling, choose
Φ(n,C)=max(0,2n−C).
(26)
The potential method now starts at Φ(0,1)=0. After every nonempty reachable state, C<2n, so the maximum equals 2n−C. There are just three cases for append:
  • First append: (0,1) becomes (1,1), so c1​=1 and c1​=1+(1−0)=2.
  • Later append without resizing: C stays fixed and n increases by one, so ΔΦ=2 and ci​=1+2=3.
  • Append to a full capacity k: (k,k) becomes (k+1,2k), so the potential changes from k to 2. Hence ci​=(k+1)+(2−k)=3, including the resize from capacity one to two.
For every n≥1, the total charge is 2+3(n−1)=3n−1, and the telescoping sum proves
T(n)=3n−1−Φ(n,Cn​)≤3n−1.
(27)
This agrees exactly with T(n)=n+Cn​−1. The unmodified choice 2n−C has initial value −1, so calling it nonnegative at the empty state would be incorrect. It also works if that initial constant is retained in the identity; alternatively, 2n−C+1 starts at zero and is nonnegative on these reachable states. The maximum above keeps a literal nonnegative credit balance from the beginning. The proof covers append alone; allowing reserve or arbitrary deletion changes the reachable states and requires a new argument.

Boolean satisfiability problem
Words: 2k Articles: 32
NP-completeness OurBigBook.com
The Boolean satisfiability problem asks whether a Boolean formula has an assignment making it true. A complete assignment is a Boolean valuation: it gives every Boolean variable a truth value, consistently at all occurrences. A satisfying assignment, also called a model of a Boolean formula, makes the entire Boolean formula true. A solver's answer SAT asserts that at least one satisfying assignment exists; UNSAT asserts that the input is an unsatisfiable Boolean formula. These are statements about existence, rather than the truth value under one particular Boolean valuation.
For conjunctive normal form, or CNF, write
F=C1​∧⋯∧Cm​,Ci​=ℓi1​∨⋯∨ℓiki​​.
(28)
Each Boolean literal ℓ is a Boolean variable or its logical negation. Each Boolean clause uses inclusive logical disjunction: one true Boolean literal suffices. The outer logical conjunction requires every Boolean clause to succeed under the same Boolean valuation. Choosing a different Boolean valuation for each Boolean clause would answer a different question.
Consider the original three-Boolean variable example
F=(x∨y)∧(¬x∨z)∧(¬y∨¬z),C1​=x∨y,C2​=¬x∨z,C3​=¬y∨¬z.
(29)
At the Boolean valuation (x,y,z)=(0,1,0), the Boolean literals in C1​ have values (0,1), those in C2​ have values (1,0), and those in C3​ have values (0,1). Every Boolean clause therefore has truth value one, so F has truth value one: this is a satisfying assignment.
The complete truth table has 23=8 Boolean valuations. Exactly two are satisfying assignments: (0,1,0) and (1,0,1). In particular, (1,1,1) satisfies the first two Boolean clauses but falsifies the third, so satisfying most Boolean clauses does not suffice for SAT. That different objective belongs to maximum satisfiability.
A short proof of completeness avoids listing all eight rows. If x=0, the Boolean clause C1​ forces y=1, after which C3​ forces z=0; C2​ is already true. If x=1, C2​ forces z=1, after which C3​ forces y=0; C1​ is already true. These two cases exhaust the truth values of x and produce precisely the two satisfying assignments above.
Verifying a satisfying assignment and finding a satisfying assignment are different tasks. Given a candidate, evaluate the Boolean formula once; finding a candidate requires choosing compatible truth values across all its Boolean clauses. The Cook-Levin theorem says that general SAT is NP-complete, even though a proposed satisfying assignment is efficiently checkable. Its proof encodes a bounded nondeterministic computation as a Boolean formula whose satisfying assignments describe accepting computations. Stephen A. Cook's 1971 paper established this connection between computational complexity theory and propositional logic.[ref]
A concrete use is checking finite configuration rules. Let x mean that an optional feature is enabled, y that a fallback is selected, and z that the feature's required component is installed. Require a feature or fallback, require the component whenever the feature is enabled, and forbid using the fallback with that component. Logical implication rewrites the second rule x→z as ¬x∨z; De Morgan's laws rewrite the third rule ¬(y∧z) as ¬y∨¬z. Their logical conjunction is exactly F, so its two satisfying assignments give the two allowed configurations. The usefulness of SAT lies in expressing local rules uniformly while demanding one globally consistent Boolean valuation. The conclusion concerns exactly these encoded rules.

Words: 256
Hazard (logic) OurBigBook.com
A logic hazard in which an output intended to remain one briefly falls to zero. In a sum of products, cover every adjacent pair of one-cells in a Karnaugh map with a common product implicant. That term omits the changing input and remains one throughout the transition, holding the OR output high regardless of the other path delays. This argument assumes one input changes at a time and the circuit starts settled.
For a concrete circuit, let x=aˉcˉ, y=bc, z=cˉd, w=y+z and q=x+w. Give every gate, including each inverter, propagation delay 10 ns. Starting from a=b=c=d=1, lower c at time zero. Signal y falls at 10 ns, while z rises only at 20 ns. Their gap passes through the two OR gates, making q fall during 30–40 ns even though its steady-state value remains one.
Adding the two consensus theorem products aˉb and bd preserves the Boolean function and holds the output high across every potentially hazardous single-input transition. The resulting five-term expression factors as q=bc+(aˉ+d)(b+cˉ). When a change of c could leave the output steadily one, b=1 and aˉ+d=1 keep the second product steadily one. In the zero-to-zero case with changing c, b=0 and aˉ+d=0 keep both output products zero. Changes of a,b,d use only one polarity each and therefore have no opposite-polarity race. This factored implementation uses three OR gates, two AND gates and two NOT gates, with a 40 ns maximum input-to-output path at the stated delays.

A combinational logic device comparing two fixed-width binary representations. For unsigned inputs a,b, a two-output encoding is L=1 exactly when a<b and G=1 exactly when a>b. Equality gives (L,G)=(0,0); (1,1) is unreachable. A one-bit implementation is L=¬a∧b, G=a∧¬b.

A digital comparator processes one pair of bits per clock cycle, storing a comparison result in a finite-state machine. Unequal upper blocks decide the order, because their difference outweighs every possible lower-block difference; equal upper blocks delegate the decision to the lower block. This is an associative operation on the three comparison outcomes. A balanced binary tree of these combinations has O(n) circuit size and O(logn) circuit depth for n-bit inputs.

A two-input logic gate whose output is one exactly when its two input bits agree. Its Boolean function is (a∧b)∨(¬a∧¬b), equivalently (a∨¬b)∧(¬a∨b). This follows by considering the two cases in which inputs are equal. It implements logical equivalence of the input truth values.

Circuit depth is the largest number of counted gates on any input-to-output path in the Boolean circuit. For an AND/OR circuit with negations on input literals, only the AND/OR gates are counted. This convention makes the restriction argument for the Linial-Mansour-Nisan theorem precise.

Boolean circuit OurBigBook.com
Given a finite acyclic Boolean circuit and its input assignment, determine the output bit. Boolean circuit evaluation is different from Circuit satisfiability problem, which asks whether some assignment succeeds.

A threshold Boolean function outputs one exactly when a weighted sum of its input bits reaches a specified threshold. The unweighted threshold function fn,r​ tests whether at least r of its n inputs are one.

Threshold function OurBigBook.com
A majority Boolean function outputs one when more than half its input bits are one. An odd number of inputs avoids a tie convention. For three bits its unique multilinear polynomial is x1​x2​+x1​x3​+x2​x3​−2x1​x2​x3​, so the polynomial method for quantum query lower bounds requires at least two exact queries.

Majority function OurBigBook.com
Its n disjoint triples give a product of degree-three multilinear polynomials, with all-variable coefficient (−2)n. Hence its degree is 3n and its exact quantum query complexity is at least ⌈3n/2⌉. At the input consisting of repeated 110 triples, each of the 2n one bits is a disjoint sensitive singleton. Thus block sensitivity is at least 2n, implying a bounded-error quantum query complexity lower bound Ω(n​).

The dual of a Boolean function f is f∗(x)=¬f(¬x). Swapping AND with OR and zero with one in a monotone circuit for f produces a circuit for f∗ by De Morgan's laws.

A circuit family (Cn​) contains one circuit for each input length n. The circuit for one length may be chosen independently of those for other lengths, so a family is a nonuniform model of computation.

Circuit family OurBigBook.com
The languages whose length-n indicator functions have Boolean circuits with at most T(n) gates for sufficiently large n, over a fixed bounded-fan-in complete basis. The family need not be constructible by one algorithm. Polynomial-size bounds give P/poly; the truth-table upper bound for circuit size applies even to undecidable languages.

Circuit size class OurBigBook.com
OR together one minterm for each accepted length-n input. Each minterm is an AND of the appropriate Boolean literals. There are at most 2n minterms, and their negated input wires can be shared, giving O(n2n) bounded-fan-in gates. This is a nonuniform existence statement, not an algorithm for determining an undecidable truth table.

Polynomial-size circuit family OurBigBook.com
For any set of lengths A, choose at length n a constant-zero Boolean circuit when n∈/A, and an AND of all inputs when n∈A. This uses O(n+1) gates. If A is undecidable, so is UA​, yet it belongs to P/poly. Since all NP languages are decidable by certificate enumeration, this proves P/poly is not equal to NP; it does not resolve containment in the other direction.

Constant-depth circuit complexity OurBigBook.com
The Håstad switching lemma says that a small-width DNF or CNF becomes representable by a shallow decision tree with high probability under a sufficiently sparse random restriction. Iterating it is a central method for proving lower bounds against constant-depth circuits.

Words: 42
Håstad switching lemma OurBigBook.com
Switching-lemma depth reduction applies the Håstad switching lemma to every bottom-layer gate, replaces each restricted gate by a shallow decision tree, and merges adjacent layers of the same gate type. Repetition reduces a constant-depth circuit to a bounded-depth decision tree while retaining many live variables.

Circuit complexity OurBigBook.com
Monotone circuit complexity studies Boolean circuits built only from AND and OR gates, without negations. Such circuits compute monotone Boolean functions, but some monotone functions require much larger monotone circuits than unrestricted circuits.
Monotone circuit
Words: 20
Monotone circuit complexity OurBigBook.com
A monotone Boolean circuit uses only AND and OR gates, variables, and optional constants. It computes a monotone Boolean function; negation gates are excluded.

Monotone circuit complexity OurBigBook.com
In the finite lattice approximation for monotone clique circuits, set m=r=⌊n1/4⌋ and ℓ=⌊log2​n⌋. A nonuniversal output accepts at most ∑s=2ℓ​s!(r−1)s(m/n)s≤2(ℓrm/n)2 of uniform positive cliques. Its missing positives require the circuit size times the positive clique error of a truncated lattice meet to be bounded below. A universal output accepts every negative colouring input; those errors require the circuit size times the negative colouring error of a forced-set closure to be at least one. Both alternatives imply the displayed superpolynomial bound by the Razborov gate-by-gate approximation lemma.

Words: 442 Articles: 7
Monotone circuit complexity OurBigBook.com
The Razborov approximation method replaces the AND and OR operations of a monotone circuit by tractable lattice operations. If each gate introduces only a controlled set of positive or negative errors, a small circuit cannot separate all positive inputs from all negative inputs.
Finite lattice approximation for monotone clique circuits
Words: 235 Articles: 2
Razborov approximation method OurBigBook.com
Take upward-closed set families of subsets of [n] of size at most ℓ, closed under the forcing rule in Razborov closure. Normalize any family containing a set of size at most one to the full family, since its clique predicate is identically true. Intersection is the meet in a lattice; closure of the union is the join in a lattice. A family represents the graphs containing a clique on at least one of its members. The approximate meet can lose positive inputs and the approximate join can acquire negative inputs. The Razborov gate-by-gate approximation lemma charges output errors to those local errors.
Negative colouring error of a forced-set closure (P(Gcolour​∈δ∨​)≤nℓ+12−r)
Words: 96
Finite lattice approximation for monotone clique circuits OurBigBook.com
Independently colour each vertex with one of m−1 colours and join differently coloured vertices. This complete multipartite graph has no m-clique. If a forced set W is rainbow but its r witnesses are not, condition on the colours of W. The disjoint petals make those failure events conditionally independent. For each witness of size at most ℓ, the probability of a colour collision is at most (2ℓ​)/(m−1). If this is at most 1/2, one closure step causes an error with probability at most 2−r. There are at most nℓ+1 possible steps; apply the union bound.

Words: 51

Choose a uniform m-subset Z and the graph consisting only of its clique. Acceptance by two approximating set families but rejection by their intersection requires two minimal witnesses whose union has size greater than ℓ. At least one has size greater than ℓ/2. The sunflower bound for minimal members of a Razborov-closed family and P(W⊆Z)≤(m/n)∣W∣ give 2∑s>ℓ/2​s!(r−1)s(m/n)s≤4qℓ/2.

Razborov approximation method OurBigBook.com
Fix integers r and l. The Razborov closure of a family of vertex sets of size at most l repeatedly adjoins a set W whenever there are r existing sets W1​,…,Wr​ whose pairwise intersections are contained in W. A family equal to its closure is called r-closed.

An inclusion-minimal s-set in an upward-closed family cannot belong to an r-member delta-system of such minimal sets: its proper core would be adjoined by Razborov closure, violating minimality. The Erdős–Rado sunflower lemma therefore bounds the number as​ of minimal s-sets. This weaker factorial bound is sufficient for the superpolynomial monotone clique lower bound.

An r-closed family has at most (r−1)k inclusion-minimal members of cardinality k. This limits the number of cliques accepted by a proper closed approximation.

The Razborov gate-by-gate approximation lemma compares a monotone circuit with the lattice computation obtained by replacing each gate by an approximate meet or join. Every disagreement at the output is charged to an error introduced by one of the circuit's gates.

The Razborov–Rudich natural-proofs barrier says that the existence of sufficiently secure pseudorandom function families rules out constructive, large properties useful against the associated circuit class.

Valiant's permanent reduction encodes satisfying assignments as cycle covers so that their weighted sum is the permanent of a matrix. Local gadgets enforce variable consistency and clause satisfaction, while signed contributions cancel invalid covers.

The variable gadget has two relevant cycle-cover states, representing the two truth values, and exposes ports that transmit the chosen value to occurrences of the variable.

The clause gadget contributes the required fixed weight precisely when at least one incident literal port represents a satisfying value.

The exclusive-or gadget connects two ports while allowing exactly one corresponding external edge to participate. Signed edge weights pair and cancel unwanted cycle covers.

A binary path-counting gadget replaces an edge of nonnegative integer weight w by a zero-one directed graph with exactly w routes from its entrance to its exit. Repeated doubling and conditional addition follow the binary expansion of w using only linearly many vertices in its bit length.

A propositional formula with two blocks of quantified Boolean variables. Prime-proof number

Words: 39
Primality testing OurBigBook.com
An integer for which replacing any one decimal numerical digit by a different digit never produces a prime number. The convention must specify whether changes creating a leading zero are permitted. An exact test enumerates the allowed substitutions and applies primality testing to each result.

Miller-Rabin primality test

Words: 78 Articles: 1
Primality testing OurBigBook.com
For an odd candidate n>3, write n−1=2sd with d odd. A base a passes when ad≡1(modn) or a2jd≡−1(modn) for some 0≤j<s; a nontrivial common divisor of a,n or failure of these conditions proves compositeness. A prime passes every base, while an odd composite passes at most one quarter of possible bases. Independent rounds give a false probable-prime probability at most 4−r. A passing composite is a strong pseudoprime, stronger than a Fermat pseudoprime.
Deterministic Miller-Rabin primality test (n<264)
Miller-Rabin primality test OurBigBook.com

The Fermat test looks for a coprime base a with aN−1≡1(modN). Such a witness proves compositeness by the Fermat little theorem, but Carmichael numbers pass for every coprime base.

A base b coprime to the tested odd composite N for which a specified probable-prime criterion passes. The sets of passing bases depend on the criterion and need not be subgroups.

The Agrawal–Biswas primality test checks the identity (X+1)n=Xn+1 modulo n and a random low-degree monic polynomial. Prime inputs always pass, while a composite input that is not a prime power fails with inverse-polynomial probability per trial.

An abstract machine specifies a computational state and rules for advancing that state without requiring one particular physical implementation. A Turing machine and a stack machine give different ways to organize the state and its transitions.

Abstract machine OurBigBook.com
A computational model with an internal state and transition rule, together with an initial state and optional observation and stopping functions. The state space need not be finite; a finite-state machine is the special case with finitely many states. A trace records observations along transitions. An interface providing only reset, update, stopping and observation operations does not by itself provide copying or rollback; a trace iterator can revisit saved observations without reversing machine effects.

A configuration of a system at one moment. In a transition system, a state is an element of its state space S, and a transition relation specifies permitted changes of state.

Postfix code

Words: 35
Stack machine OurBigBook.com
Code whose operand-producing instructions precede the instruction that consumes those operands. A stack machine can translate a binary program expression by producing its left operand, producing its right operand, and then applying the operation to the two top values.

Optimal stack evaluation of a binary expression tree (d(e∘f)=min{max(d(e),1+d(f)),max(d(f),1+d(e))})

Words: 167
Stack machine OurBigBook.com
Suppose each subtree of a binary expression tree is evaluated completely before its sibling, leaves one result on an operand stack, and is not spilled or interleaved. If the child depths are p,q, evaluating the first child needs p slots and keeping its result while evaluating the second needs 1+q. Reversing the order gives max(q,1+p). If either order preserves the expression's meaning, the minimum is max(p,q) when p=q and p+1 when p=q. For example, if p>q, integrality gives p≥q+1, so evaluating the deeper child first attains the lower bound p. If p=q, the second child needs its own p slots plus one saved result regardless of order. Induction over the binary expression tree proves optimality in this evaluation model.
For a noncommutative operator, an instruction swapping the top two stack entries or a reverse-operand opcode permits the same ordering while preserving operand positions. Reordering still requires absence of order-sensitive side effects. Reassociation and interleaving are separate transformations and are not part of this optimality claim.
